newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Council accord on satellite communications networks seen.
newsitem.headline: Council accord on satellite communications networks seen.

text.p: The Telecommunications Council is expected to reach a political agreement on Friday on a watered-down proposal on authorising satellite personal communications systems in the EU, diplomats said.

The Council in June rejected the Commission's original draft decision, COM(95)529, to set up a single EU system for selecting the limited number of networks that will be able to offer telephone and data-transmission services via satellite.
But diplomats said member states were close to agreement on a new text that would give a primary role to the European Conference for Postal and Telecommunications Administrations (CEPT).

CEPT, a pan-European inter-governmental body, would be asked to agree by mid-1997 a plan for harmonising the EU's approach to using radio frequencies and authorising the satellite communications systems that operate in the EU.
The EU would act only if CEPT did not make satisfactory progress.
Most member states objected to the original text because it would have authorised the Commission to draw up criteria for licensing operators and to play a major role in selecting the operators.

The Commission argued that the EU needed to develop a united front, warning that the EU could be bound by decisions made elsewhere, especially the United States -- which has already licensed several personal communications systems that are poised to set up global operations by the end of the decade.
They include Globalstar, led by U.S. companies Qualcomm Inc and Loral Corp; Iridium, led by the U.S.'s Motorola Inc; and Odyssey, with Canada's Teleglobe Inc and the U.S.'s TRW Inc.

But EU governments argued that enough coordination already took place through organisations such as the CEPT and International Telecommunications Union and that no special EU effort was needed since the number of satellite networks would be small.

The compromise text leaves the final decision to authorise satellite personal communications networks up to national governments. But it asks them to coordinate their procedures if the number of operators must be limited because of a shortage of frequencies.
